questions.objective: Calculate real size and convert units
questions.Foundation: The recorded image length is 24 mm and the magnification is ×600. Calculate the real cell length in micrometres. Use real length = image length ÷ magnification, and 1 mm = 1000 micrometres. Show working.
questions.Higher: The recorded image length is 72 mm and the magnification is ×24 000. Calculate the real cell length in metres. Give the answer in standard form and show working.
questions.markingFoundation: 24 ÷ 600 = 0.04 mm, or a correct equivalent rearrangement (1); valid mm-to-micrometre conversion, ×1000 (1); 40 µm (1). Fully correct answer with unit can earn 3. A correct calculation method with arithmetic error can retain method/conversion credit; do not give an answer mark for dimensional confusion.
questions.markingHigher: 72 ÷ 24000 = 0.003 mm, or equivalent valid method (1); valid conversion from mm to m, ÷1000 (1); 3 × 10⁻⁶ m in standard form (1). Accept 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. Fully correct answer/unit can earn 3. A correct method/conversion can retain those marks despite arithmetic error. A correct non-standard-form decimal earns up to 2/3, because standard form is requested.

questions.Foundation: The two observation drawings in F-DRAWING are from different specimens. Explain why their displayed lengths cannot be used to decide which cell was really larger.
questions.Higher: A student writes “actual cell length = 4 cm” by measuring a magnified drawing on a screen. Explain one change needed for a valid size record.
questions.markingFoundation: The drawings have no calibrated scale/magnification, so displayed lengths cannot establish real lengths (1). Accept that the drawings may have different unknown magnifications. Do not credit simply saying that they look different.
questions.markingHigher: Use the known magnification/calibrated scale to calculate actual size, or include a correctly calibrated scale bar rather than treating displayed size as real size (1).

questions.objective: Recall the relationship between DNA, genes and chromosomes

questions.markingFoundation: A chromosome is made of DNA and carries many genes.
questions.markingHigher: Chromosomes normally occur in pairs and each carries many genes.
optionsFoundation: Each chromosome carries exactly one gene
A chromosome is made of DNA and carries many genes
A chromosome is made of genes but contains no DNA
optionsHigher: Chromosomes normally occur in pairs and each carries many genes
All genes occur on a single chromosome in every body cell
Chromosomes are produced only after the cytoplasm divides
questions.correctOptionFoundation: A chromosome is made of DNA and carries many genes
questions.correctOptionHigher: Chromosomes normally occur in pairs and each carries many genes

questions.Foundation: Before mitosis, a cell grows and increases its sub-cellular structures. Describe what happens to its DNA before mitosis and what happens to chromosomes/nuclei during mitosis.
questions.Higher: Explain why the two new nuclei formed by mitosis normally contain the same genes as the original nucleus.
questions.markingFoundation: DNA replicates to make two copies of each chromosome (1); sets of chromosomes separate to opposite ends and nuclei divide (1). No named mitotic phases required.
questions.markingHigher: DNA is replicated beforehand, producing copies of each chromosome (1); each new nucleus receives one copy of each chromosome / an identical complete chromosome set (1). Do not require cytoplasm division for this question about nuclei. Do not credit a claim that DNA merely grows bigger or that each new nucleus receives only half the original types of gene.

questions.Foundation: F-CILIATED shows a cell from an unfamiliar water animal. Its hair-like projections beat to move liquid, and it contains many mitochondria. Explain how the mitochondria help it do this.
questions.Higher: Figure H-NERVE shows a cell transmitting signals from the spinal cord to a foot. It has a long extension and branched ends. Explain how both features help its function.
questions.markingFoundation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration (1); this releases energy needed for the beating/movement of the projections (1). Accept respiration releases the energy for movement without the word aerobic. Do not award a mark just for repeating that there are many mitochondria. Energy is released, not created.
questions.markingHigher: Long extension carries signals over a long distance (1); branches connect with other cells/allow communication to several cells (1). Information about signal transmission is provided; do not require untaught synapse chemistry.

questions.Foundation: State one cell type adult bone-marrow stem cells can form. State how embryonic stem cells differ in the range of cells they can form.

questions.markingHigher: Embryonic stem cells can form most human cell types (1); meristem stem cells can form any type of plant cell throughout plant life (1). Do not infer human–plant interchangeability.

questions.objective: Evaluate a stem-cell proposal using supplied evidence
questions.Foundation: A research team proposes further work on the treatment in F-STEM-TABLE. Explain one reason to continue the research and one reason it may not be suitable for every patient.
questions.Higher: Use H-STEM-TABLE. A nursery claims that meristem cloning guarantees the long-term survival of this rare plant. Evaluate the claim using one evidence-based benefit and one limitation.
questions.markingFoundation: Replacing damaged nerve cells could help restore lost function, supporting further research (1); viral transfer could harm a patient, or embryo use could make treatment unacceptable to a patient with a justified ethical/religious objection (1). Link the table evidence to a consequence or suitability judgement; simply copying two entries without a reason is insufficient. Do not require proof of effectiveness or imply a guaranteed cure.
questions.markingHigher: Rapid production of many plants can increase numbers/preserve the existing useful resistance, supporting conservation in the short term (1); genetic uniformity can leave the clones susceptible to a different/new disease, so long-term survival is not guaranteed (1). Accept another defensible limitation based on the supplied evidence. A bare yes/no judgement earns no separate mark.

questions.Foundation: A model cell is a cube with side length 2 mm. Calculate its surface-area-to-volume ratio. Use surface area = 6 × side² and volume = side³. Show working.
questions.Higher: Model cell P is a cube with side length 0.5 mm. Model cell Q has surface-area-to-volume ratio 3:1, measured using mm. Calculate P’s ratio and state how many times as large as Q’s it is.
questions.markingFoundation: Valid surface-area/volume method: 6×2² and 2³, yielding 24 mm² and 8 mm³ if arithmetic is correct (1); correct ratio 3:1 or an equivalent ratio such as 24:8 (1). The question does not require simplest form, so a correct equivalent final ratio can earn 2. If earlier arithmetic is wrong, award at most the method mark; do not award full marks merely for simplifying a wrong ratio consistently. Do not credit area/volume dimensional confusion.
questions.markingHigher: P has surface area 1.5 mm² and volume 0.125 mm³, giving SA:V = 12:1 or an equivalent ratio (1); 12 ÷ 3 = four times Q (1). If P is wrong through arithmetic but a consistent valid comparison P÷3 is shown, allow only the comparison mark by error carried forward, for a maximum of 1/2. Do not credit a reversed comparison or invalid dimensions.

questions.objective: Explain adaptations of an exchange surface
questions.Foundation: Figure F-GILL shows many thin folds with a good blood supply. Explain how two of these features increase gas exchange.
questions.Higher: Figure H-LEAF shows a thin leaf with many air spaces and stomata. Explain how two features make diffusion of carbon dioxide to photosynthesising cells effective.
questions.markingFoundation: Any two distinct feature–effect links (1 each): folds increase area; thin surface shortens diffusion distance; blood flow maintains concentration gradient. Simply naming features gets no explanation marks.
questions.markingHigher: Any two distinct links (1 each): thin leaf short diffusion path; air spaces create large internal area/short paths; stomata allow gas exchange with surrounding air. Do not require guard-cell regulation or later plant physiology.

questions.Foundation: Figure F-ION shows mineral-ion concentration 0.4 units outside a root hair and 2.0 units inside, with uptake into the cell. Explain how uptake can continue.
questions.Higher: H-GLUCOSE shows glucose uptake from the small intestine into blood. A treatment reduces respiration in the intestinal lining cells; the concentration difference initially stays unchanged. Predict the effect on continued uptake and explain why.
questions.markingFoundation: Active transport moves ions from lower to higher concentration / against their gradient (1); requires energy from respiration (1).

Accept equivalent conditional wording. Do not infer that all respiration or all passive transport stops. No advanced cotransport mechanism is required.

questions.objective: Calculate percentage change of plant-tissue mass
questions.Foundation: This is a separate pilot batch, not the tissue used for 7b. Use F-MASS-TABLE to calculate the percentage change in mass. Use (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100. Include the sign and show working.
questions.Higher: This is a separate pilot batch, not the tissue used for 7b. Use H-MASS-TABLE to calculate the percentage change in mass. Give your answer to one decimal place, including its sign, and show working.
questions.markingFoundation: (2.64 − 2.40) ÷ 2.40 × 100 (1); +10% (1). A fully correct signed final answer can earn 2 without written working. Award the method mark for a valid percentage-change method even if arithmetic goes wrong. A gain stated in words with 10% is acceptable; 0.24 g alone is not a percentage.
questions.markingHigher: (2.92 − 3.20) ÷ 3.20 × 100 = −8.75% (1 for valid method); −8.8% to one decimal place (1). A correct signed, rounded answer can earn 2. Accept 8.8% loss in words. −8.75% shows the correct method but misses the requested rounding, so 1/2. Do not double-penalise a sign error within the method.

questions.objective: Interpret osmosis evidence and improve an investigation
questions.Foundation: The table and graph show celeriac tissue results. The investigator used one cylinder per concentration, did not blot before final weighing, and used different soaking times. They claim “every plant tissue has no net mass change at 0.40 mol/dm³”. Evaluate the claim. Use the graph and osmosis, then describe how you would improve the investigation to test the claim.
questions.Higher: Use H-OSM-TABLE and H-OSM-GRAPH. The investigator used one cylinder per concentration, did not blot before final weighing, and varied soaking time. They claim that every type of plant tissue has no net mass change at exactly the same sucrose concentration. Evaluate the claim. Use an estimate from the graph and osmosis, and propose an improved investigation.
questions.markingFoundation: Use the original level-of-response rubric in the blueprint: 0–6, human review. Indicative content: zero net mass change at about 0.40 for this tissue/conditions; positive/negative mass changes from net water movement across partially permeable membranes; single cylinders, surface liquid, different durations undermine comparison; equal dimensions/same tissue, equal time/temperature/solution volume, consistent gentle blotting, replicates and means, more concentrations near zero; do not generalise to all plant tissue or claim water stops moving. Explicitly credit comparing several plant tissue types across the concentration range under matched conditions (dimensions, time, temperature, solution volume and blotting), with repeats within each type and comparison of their estimated zero-change concentrations. Repeats of one tissue assess reliability but cannot establish the same zero-change concentration for every plant tissue; even agreement among several types cannot prove a universal claim.
questions.markingHigher: Human best-fit level marking, 0–6: estimate the zero near 0.32 mol/dm³ for this tissue/conditions; explain net water movement through partially permeable membranes; use the lack of replicates, unremoved surface liquid and varied time to question the universal/exact claim; propose justified controlled repeats, means and additional concentrations near zero. Do not demand knowledge of water-potential equations or an exact intracellular solute concentration. Explicitly credit comparing several plant tissue types across the concentration range under matched conditions (dimensions, time, temperature, solution volume and blotting), with repeats within each type and comparison of their estimated zero-change concentrations. Repeats of one tissue assess reliability but cannot establish the same zero-change concentration for every plant tissue; even agreement among several types cannot prove a universal claim.
